newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - Natgas seen supporting GSCI/CRB in winter.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - Natgas seen supporting GSCI/CRB in winter.

text.p: While surging oil prices are helping boost returns on investments in commodities, as measured by the Goldman Sachs Commodity Index (GSCI) and the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau Index (CRB), the place of natural gas in a commodity portfolio should not be ignored going into the winter, analysts said.
"The dynamic in this area has changed dramatically with the recent divergence between oil and natural gas markets," Smith Barney analyst John Saucer said.
"The competition between fuels now greatly favors natural gas as we head into the winter season."
NYMEX November natgas futures expire on October 25, leaving December as the active month and the contract was up 3.9 cents at $2.615 per million British thermal units (mmBtu) midday Monday.
December natgas has recovered from late summer lows at $1.735 mmBtu on September 8 to a high of $2.590 on October 13.
"Protracted cold like that of the 1995/96 winter, the odds for which are limited, could produce gas prices in excess of $3.50 mmBtu," Merrill Lynch analyst Michael Rothman said.
Last winter nearby natgas futures prices saw an all time record high at $3.720 mmBtu.
Natgas has a 12.25 percent weighting in the GSCI and a 5.94 pct weighting in the CRB.
The GSCI was up 0.21 points at 211.07 midday and the CRB was up 0.40 points at 243.75.
"The energy sector continues to be the star of the show and there is little incentive to alter our bullish rating," Merrill Lynch strategist Bill O'Neill said.

In the summer, milder-than-normal temperatures in the main natgas consumption areas of the U.S. Midwest and Northeast cut utility cooling requirements, allowing natgas storage to rebuild at a faster-than-expected pace, analysts said.
"But the nation as a whole is still set to enter the 1996-97 winter with the lowest working gas storage levels ever," Saucer warned.

"We expect betweeen 2,725-2,775 bcf (billion cubic feet) of supply in US working gas storage on November 1, compared with last year's 2,988 bcf and the 3,000 bcf widely considered to be the norm," Saucer said.
For the week ended October 11 working gas in storage stood at 2,607 billion cubic feet (bcf), 261 bcf below a year-ago.
"This, in turn, leaves the market vulnerable to both physical and psychological pressure in the event of normal to colder-than-normal winter weather," Rothman said.
Better demand prospects, tied to the impending winter heating season and fuel switching to cheaper natgas by utilties, may also boost natgas prices, analysts said.

The mild U.S. summer saw natgas demand slump to 43.4 bcf per day, 10 pct below year-ago levels, but analysts expect demand to pick back up to around 62 bcf a day, in line with 1995, in the fourth quarter.
"The important point is that the demand outlook in the fourth quarter is likely to be enhanced by the current gas-fuel relationship," Saucer said.

In early October natgas in the US Gulf Coast was trading around $2.10-2.20 mmBtu, while crude oil was trading at the equivalent of $4.30 mmBtu, spot heating oil at $3.15 mmBtu and 1.0 pct sulfur fuel oil at $3.15 mmBtu.

"With the oil complex well supported by tight pre-winter distillate (diesel and heating oil) supplies, a narrowing of the huge spread between gas and oil is likely to come more from adjustments on gas than adjustments on oil," Saucer said.
No help is likely on the supply side of the equation either, analysts said.
Growth in U.S. dry gas production has been negative during the first three quarters of this year.
Average production of 50.9 bcf a day in the first nine months of the year was off 1.2 pct from year-ago levels, and in the third quarter 1996, production of 48.7 bcf was down 4.3 pct from 1995.
